definition: In historical psychology, content means whatever is present in consciousness when considered apart from its form, relations, or implications, and it can also mean any constituent of an experienced whole. The term was used as a neutral way to refer to what is in the mind, whether felt, perceived, or willed.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Content; pinned source text

reasons: The definition says content “can also mean whatever is present in consciousness … and it can also mean any constituent of an experienced whole.” While the first part matches the packet’s (1), the “experienced whole” phrasing is not directly supported by the packet’s wording (it instead says “total consciousness” and “presented whole” / “presented whole”).

The definition states the neutral usage refers to what is in the mind “whether felt, perceived, or willed,” but the packet specifically lists “'felt,' 'presented,' 'willed' content” and does not mention “perceived.”
